section.title: The Springtime Invitation
section.sectionRationale: The bride hears her beloved coming, leaping over the hills like a young stag, and he calls her out into the new world of spring: the winter is past, the flowers have appeared, arise and come away. This movement is one of the most joyful in the Song, a picture of love that summons the beloved into life and openness, guarded by a shared care to keep the little foxes from spoiling the vineyard.
section.thesis: Love comes seeking, calls the beloved out of winter into springtime, and asks to be guarded from the small things that spoil it; the bride answers with the confession of mutual belonging, my beloved is mine and I am his.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the beloved’s approach, leaping over the mountains to the window; his springtime invitation, arise and come away, for the winter is past; and the shared guarding of the vineyard against the little foxes, sealed by the refrain of belonging.

verses.text: Listen! My {{dodi|beloved}} approaches. Look! Here he comes, leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills.
My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Look, he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattice.
My beloved calls to me, “Arise, my {{raya|darling}}. Come away with me, my beautiful one.
For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.
The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land.
The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance. Arise, come away, my darling; come away with me, my beautiful one.”
O my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the crevices of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is lovely.
Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in bloom.
My {{dodi|beloved}} is mine and I am his; he pastures his flock among the lilies.
Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of Bether.

dodi.gloss: Beloved, the bride’s characteristic name for her man, my beloved, dodi. It recurs like a refrain through the Song and reaches its height in the confession of mutual belonging, my beloved is mine and I am his.

raya.gloss: My darling, literally my companion or dear friend, the bridegroom’s recurring name for the bride. Here it opens his springtime call: arise, my darling, and come away.

basic.context: The bride hears her beloved coming from far off, bounding over the hills like a young stag, and he arrives at the window and calls her out. Winter is over, he says, the flowers are up, the birds are singing, so arise and come away with me. The lovers agree to guard their blossoming vineyard from the little foxes that spoil it, and she sums up their love in a line the whole Song remembers: my beloved is mine and I am his.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a poem of invitation, and its power lies in the picture of love that comes seeking. On the plain level it is the joy of a man calling his beloved into the open delight of spring. Read within the whole Bible, it also carries the note of a greater voice that calls His people out of winter into life. Both readings honor the text; the second grows out of the first.
basic.originalLanguages: The two pet names carry the scene: the bride’s dodi, my beloved, who comes leaping over the hills, and his raya, my darling, whom he calls to arise. The invitation, arise and come away, is a summons out of hiding and into the shared, blossoming world of love.
basic.typology: Love that comes seeking and calls the beloved out of winter pictures the God who comes to His people and summons them into life. The little foxes that ruin the vineyard picture the small compromises that spoil love if they are not caught early.
basic.christ: The Bridegroom who leaps over the hills, stands at the window, and calls, arise and come away, echoes the Christ who seeks His people, calls them by name out of death’s winter, and bids them come to Him. His voice is the one that turns winter into spring.
basic.god: God is a seeking God, who comes to His people rather than waiting at a distance, and who calls them into joy and openness. He also cares about the vineyard, the small foxes matter to Him, for love is guarded in the details.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:3 to 4, the good Shepherd calls His own by name and they follow. Song 6:3 repeats the belonging refrain. 1 Corinthians 15:54 to 57, the winter of death is finally past in Christ.
basic.oneStory: The springtime call is love’s summons out of winter into life. It sings of a man calling his beloved, and it whispers of the God who comes seeking, calls His people out of death, and brings them into the endless spring of His presence.

context.literary:
This poem is carefully built. It opens with the woman's report, 'Listen! My beloved approaches,' 2:8, so the whole scene is seen and heard through her. For six verses she watches him come: across mountains, to the wall, to the window, to the lattice. The distance closes in steps. Then, at 2:10, the report gives way to his own voice, which she quotes. She is the narrator of his invitation, and the invitation fills verses 10 to 14.

The invitation itself has a clear shape. It begins and ends with the same call, 'Arise, my darling... come away,' 2:10 and 2:13, and between the two calls come reasons: the winter is over, the flowers are out, the birds are singing, the fig tree and the vines are fragrant. The two calls make a frame around a description of spring, so the call is held up by evidence in the landscape. Verse 14 adds a second address, to 'my dove,' and moves from the outer world to her face and voice.

Verses 15 to 17 change the mood and the speaker. Verse 15 is a small, difficult couplet about foxes. Verse 16 is her confession of belonging. Verse 17 is her answer to his invitation, a request that he turn. The movement therefore goes from his coming, to his call, to her reply, and the reply is more guarded than the call. She does not at once leap out of the window.

This movement is the second of the Song's major sections. Chapter 1 ended with a request for rest under his arm and a charge to leave love undisturbed. Here the love is not put to sleep but moves outdoors, and the next movement, 3:1-5, returns to night. The poem alternates between day and night, outside and inside, presence and absence, and this movement is the brightest of them.
context.historical:
The poem draws on the climate of the land. In Israel the winter rains fall from about November to March, and the flowers, birds and fruit that follow in the spring were a welcome sign of the year's turn. 'The rain is over and gone' describes the end of that season. The turtledove and the other migrating birds return in spring, and the prophet Jeremiah says that the turtledove knows 'her appointed seasons,' Jeremiah 8:7. A hearer in Israel would read the verses as a calendar, and the fig tree putting out its first fruit, and the vines in flower, as the markers of the best weeks of the year.

The lover's behavior also reflects the customs of courtship. A young man could not simply walk into a woman's house, and so he stands outside, behind the wall, looking in at the lattice. The wall and the window are the bounds of her family's home, The lattice in Proverbs 7:6 is where a watchful teacher looks out, so the poem uses a setting that wisdom literature knows from the other side.

The 'clefts of the rock' and 'crevices of the cliff,' 2:14, are the high, steep places where wild doves nest, and Jeremiah 48:28 pictures a dove nesting at the mouth of a cave. The dove is shy and hidden, and the lover's wish to see her face reflects the way a hidden bird is hard to coax into the open.

Vineyards were central to Israel's economy and also to its poetry, as in Isaiah 5:1, where a beloved has a vineyard on a very fertile hill. Foxes, or jackals, dug under the vines and ate the grapes, so a vineyard in bloom needed watching. The little animals that spoil it are a farmer's real worry.
context.canonical:
The central image, a lover who comes calling at the house, finds echoes across Scripture. The Lord tells His people that He stands at the door and knocks, Revelation 3:20, and Jesus says that the shepherd 'calls his own sheep by name and leads them out,' John 10:3. Both pictures fit the Song's bridegroom, who comes to the window and says, 'Arise... come away.' The New Testament does not quote the poem, but it knows the shape of the story.

The call to come away uses the same verb construction that God used to Abram, 'go,' Genesis 12:1, a command that sets someone out on a journey to a new life. The bride is called out of one place into another by someone who loves her. Ezekiel says that God found Israel in her blood and made her His own, and Hosea has God lead Israel out into the wilderness to speak tenderly to her. In each case the love comes first and the calling follows.

The winter-to-spring pattern also has a place in the larger story. Isaiah says that the desert will 'rejoice and blossom like a rose,' Isaiah 35:1. Paul writes that death is swallowed up in victory, 1 Corinthians 15:54, and Revelation promises that 'the former things have passed away,' Revelation 21:4. The poem's 'winter is past' is the human form of a hope that the whole creation shares.

The foxes of 2:15 have a counterpart in the prophets' accusation, 'Your prophets, O Israel, are like foxes among the ruins,' Ezekiel 13:4, where foxes are things that live off what is damaged. And the closing confession, 2:16, is quoted back and reversed at 6:3 and gives way to a plainer form at 7:10, 'I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.' The Song's own canon within the canon is a story of belonging that deepens.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants the first hearers to feel what it is like to be sought. The whole scene is made of eager movement on his side, leaping and bounding and peering, and of patience, because he waits at the wall and asks gently. The hearers are meant to see that real love takes the first step and does not coerce.

The poet also wants them to link love with the renewing of the world. A courtship in springtime is the poem's way of saying that delight in a person and delight in creation belong together. A people who lived by the seasons would hear the lines as saying that love, too, has a season, and this is the season of its blossoming. That prepares for the charge at the end of the previous movement, that love comes at its proper time.

The poet then adds a note of care. A relationship in bloom is vulnerable, and the foxes in 2:15 are the small things that can ruin it. The hearers are to guard what is good before it is damaged. The poem puts a warning in the middle of a celebration, and it means to be heard: it is easier to keep a vineyard than to restore it.

Finally, the confession of belonging, 2:16, is meant to be the center. All the movement of the poem is a way of getting to those words, and the first hearers were to see that love ends in mutual possession, not in conquest.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem describes a lover's call, and it does not prescribe courtship customs. It would be a mistake to turn the picture of a man at a window into a rule for how a suitor should behave. What the poem commends is the character it shows: eagerness, gentleness, patience and respect for the one he calls.

The one near-command in the passage is the request about the foxes, 2:15, and the speaker and the hearers are not clearly fixed, so it is better read as a wise proverb than as a legislated rule: guard what is blossoming. That matches the wisdom tradition, where small neglect is often said to ruin a great good, and it can be applied to marriage, friendship and a congregation alike.

The invitation to 'come away' is not a model of how to treat God's call in every detail, and the poem is not a command to leave home. But it does show the shape of a response to love, which is to be moved to come out and not to hide. The believer who hears the call of Christ is invited into the open, and the application is to answer, not to copy the setting of a window and a wall.

debates.question: What are the 'little foxes' of 2:15?

views.label: Small faults that spoil love
views.case: The most common reading takes the foxes as a figure for minor offenses, careless words, neglect and quarrels, that eat away a young relationship. The image fits the vineyard, which the poem has already used for the woman, and the word 'little' underlines that the trouble is in the small things.

views.label: Rivals or intruders
views.case: Others take the foxes as suitors or outside threats who might spoil the couple's vineyard, since the bride's brothers have been hostile, 1:6, and the vineyard is a picture of the woman. The plural imperative, 'Catch for us,' suggests that others are asked to help guard it.

views.label: A fragment of a work song
views.case: Some think the verse is a quoted vineyard song, a bit of a folk tune about catching foxes, which the poet works into the scene. On this view the verse is not a coded warning and should be read as a light moment.

debates.bearing: The text does not explain the image, so a firm claim would go beyond it. All three readings agree that the vineyard is in bloom and in danger, and the passage invites care. The first reading is the one that most easily carries over into marriage, friendship and the church.

debates.question: What does she ask in 2:17?

views.label: Come back to me until dawn
views.case: On this reading she asks him to turn and return like a gazelle over the 'rugged mountains' before the day breaks and the shadows flee, so that the night is spent together. The footnote 'rugged mountains' supports reading the last words as a place name or a description of rough terrain.

views.label: Go away until evening
views.case: Others take 'turn' as a request that he depart, leaving until the cool of the evening, when the shadows lengthen. The Hebrew phrase about the day 'breathing' can mean the evening breeze.

views.label: A deliberately open verse
views.case: Some say the poem leaves the verse open on purpose, so that it carries the bride's mix of wanting him near and wanting him free. The 'turn' is a call that has not yet been answered.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity matters little for the main point, because in all three readings the bride's reply is the eager return of love. It also shows how the poem moves from the day scene to the night scene that follows in chapter 3.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verbs of the lover's approach are vivid. At 2:8 he is 'leaping' across the mountains and 'bounding' over the hills. The Hebrew uses two verbs, a participle of qafaz and a participle of dalag, which are verbs of springing and skipping. The effect is of a man who cannot walk but must run. The comparison with a gazelle, tzevi, and a young stag, ofer ha'ayalim, appears again at the end, 2:17, framing the whole scene with the lover as a graceful, fast creature.

At 2:10 and again at 2:13 the call is qumi lakh... ulekhi lakh, 'arise... go for yourself.' The second verb is a command to go, in the same form as God's word to Abram in Genesis 12:1, lekh lekha. The Song does not quote Genesis, but the form is the same, so the call carries the sense of a departure that opens a new life. The extra 'for yourself,' lakh, is a pronoun that makes the going her own: she is not dragged but invited.

In 2:12 the BSB gives 'the season of singing has come,' and the footnote adds 'Or pruning.' The Hebrew zamir can mean song and, from a related verb, to prune a vine. The word is therefore double. In a vineyard poem, the lover may be saying that it is the season of singing and the season of pruning, the work of care. The poet may have chosen the word for both senses, and the footnote shows that translators noticed.

At 2:14 he calls her 'my dove,' yonati, and says that she is in the cleft of the rock, chagvei hasela. A different Hebrew word for a cleft is used in Exodus 33:22, where God puts Moses in a cleft of the rock to shelter him, so the words are not the same. But the pictures are kin: a rock cleft is a place of hiding and also of safety.

At 2:15 the foxes are shu'alim, a word that covers foxes and jackals, and they are 'little,' qetannim. The verb 'catch,' echezu, is plural, which is why the speaker is unclear. At 2:16 the confession is dodi li va'ani lo, 'my beloved is mine and I am his,' with her claim on him first. At 6:3 the order is reversed, ani ledodi vedodi li, 'I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine,' and at 7:10 she says, in the BSB's words, 'I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.' The word for desire there, teshuqah, appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7 and here. At 7:10 the curse of Genesis 3:16 is reversed: desire that was a source of strain is a sign of love.

Finally, 2:17's 'before the day breaks' translates a phrase about the day 'breathing,' yafuach hayom, a picture of the cool breeze of daybreak or evening. The mountains of Bether, har bater, come from a root meaning to cut or divide, which is why the BSB footnote gives 'the rugged mountains.'

typology.fulfillment: In the Song the man comes to her, over the mountains and to the window. In the Bible's larger story, God comes to His people: He walks in the garden seeking Adam, Genesis 3:8-9, and the Son comes 'to seek and to save the lost,' as Jesus says of Himself, Luke 19:10. Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom, Matthew 9:15. The escalation is that the one who comes is not only willing but able to do what He calls for, since He gave Himself for His bride, Ephesians 5:25. The type falls short because the lover in the Song is a man who waits at a wall, while the Bridegroom enters the world and goes to the cross.

typology.type: Winter past, the season of singing
typology.fulfillment: The lover's 'now the winter is past' pictures a change of seasons that the New Testament applies to the new age. Death has been 'swallowed up in victory,' 1 Corinthians 15:54, and the Lord is the one who will make 'all things new,' Revelation 21:5. Isaiah's desert that blossoms, Isaiah 35:1, is another form of the same hope. The escalation is that the Song's spring comes and goes with the calendar, while the spring of the new creation does not. The type falls short in that it is only a taste, and the winter in the poem will return.

The beloved's voice draws her from hiding. Jesus says that the shepherd 'calls his own sheep by name and leads them out,' John 10:3, and when He called out 'Lazarus, come out!' the dead man came, John 11:43. The correspondence is that a voice from outside is what brings someone to move, and the escalation is that Christ's voice does not only invite but gives life, Ephesians 2:1. The type falls short because the bride in the Song could stay behind the wall, while the dead cannot answer until they are called.

typology.type: The little foxes in the vineyard
typology.fulfillment: The vineyard is a common picture of God's people, Isaiah 5:1, and it is a place that can be spoiled by small things. In the New Testament the same care is commanded of a church: the Lord's people are to guard the flock against what would damage it. The correspondence is that blossoms need protection. The type falls short because the poem does not say what the foxes are, and the New Testament provides the guard, the Shepherd who keeps those who are His.

study.christ:
The New Testament says plainly that Christ is the bridegroom, Matthew 9:15, John 3:29, and the Song's second movement lets that picture speak in the voice of a man who comes to a window. The reader of the Gospels will recognize the pattern: a person who is outside comes toward those inside, stands where He can be heard and speaks. The Lord says, 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock,' Revelation 3:20. In the Song the lover stands behind the wall, and the poem makes a point of his waiting.

What he says is not a demand but an invitation based on a change that has already happened. 'For now the winter is past,' 2:11. The call is made on the ground of a finished work. That is the shape of the gospel. Christ does not call people to come in order to end the winter. He calls them because the winter has ended: the penalty is paid, the rain of judgment is over, and the season of singing has come. 'Come to Me,' He says, 'and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28. The reasons are given first, and then the call is made.

The beloved also calls her 'my dove in the clefts of the rock.' The picture of a hiding person who is invited out is a picture of the sinner in shame. After the fall Adam and Eve hid, and God came looking, Genesis 3:8-9. Here too the hidden one is sought and addressed with affection, and the lover asks only to see her face and hear her voice. Christ's way with the ashamed is the same. He does not summon them to be punished, He seeks them out and welcomes them.

Then comes the confession, 'My beloved is mine and I am his,' 2:16. Her words give the believer a way to speak of Christ. The first claim is that He is hers, and the second that she is His. The gospel works the same way: Christ gives Himself to those who believe, and they are His. Paul says that 'you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3. And the Bridegroom's belonging is not cold. 'He pastures his flock among the lilies' pictures a shepherd who is content among beauty, and John 10:14 has Jesus say, 'I know My sheep and My sheep know Me.'

The final verse, 2:17, in which she asks him to turn and return before the day breaks, echoes the church's longing for the return of Christ. It is a poem for the present age, between the invitation and the full day. A caution: not every detail of the poem, the gazelle or the lattice, is a code, and the New Testament does not claim it is. The poem's chief gift is a pattern: the Bridegroom who comes, calls and keeps.
study.god:
The Song shows God by analogy, in the form of a lover, and so it requires care. What it makes visible is a pattern of divine love that the rest of Scripture states directly. First, God is the one who takes the first step. The man comes to the wall and the window, and the bride does not have to find a path to him. The Bible's story is that God sought Adam in the garden, Genesis 3:9, and sent His Son, John 14:18, 'I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.' Love begins on God's side.

Second, God is patient. The lover waits at the lattice and asks. He does not break in. The God of the Bible stands at the door and knocks, Revelation 3:20, and He says to His people, 'I will not forget you,' Isaiah 49:15. This does not make Him weak. It shows that His power is joined to a respect for those He calls, and that His love seeks a free answer.

Third, God is a God of seasons. The poem sets love against the turn of the year, and the Bible does the same with the purposes of God: there is a time for every deed, Ecclesiastes 3:17, and a fullness of time. A God who made winter and spring is not hurried, and He is not late. The believer can wait for a season without thinking that God has forgotten.

Fourth, God cares about small things. The poem does not neglect the foxes. In the same way the Lord notices the details of His people's lives, and the LORD says of His vineyard, 'I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it,' Isaiah 27:3. The love that is large enough to call a person out of winter is also close enough to guard the blossom.

The poem holds in tension the eagerness of the lover and the freedom of the beloved. God is not indifferent to whether we come, and He does not force us. For worship, this means that the proper response to God's call is neither fear nor a cold duty. It is a glad movement toward Someone who has first moved toward us, and the believer's confession, 'My beloved is mine and I am his,' is a form of praise: 1 John 4:19, 'We love because He first loved us.'

crossReferences.note: The belonging refrain returns with the order reversed: 'I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me.' In 2:16 she first claims him and then gives herself. By 6:3 she begins with herself. The change shows love maturing from delight in being possessed to rest in being given.

The refrain reaches its simplest form: 'I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.' The word for desire here is the one in Genesis 3:16 and 4:7. The strain of the fall is replaced by a desire that is received gladly, and the poem ends the belonging refrain on that note.

Another scene of the lover at the door: 'My beloved is knocking.' Here she delays, and he is gone when she opens. The contrast with 2:8-10 is sobering. The same man who calls in the spring is missed in the night when he is not answered at once.

'I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard.' The prophet uses the same word for beloved and the same vineyard picture, but in his song the vineyard yields wild grapes. The Song shows the vineyard as it should be, in bloom and guarded.

'Even the stork in the sky knows her appointed seasons. The turtledove... keep their time of migration.' The turtledove in Song 2:12 knows when spring has come. The prophet says that God's people do not know their season. The poem's birds are a quiet reproach and an invitation.

Moab is told to be 'like a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave.' The dove in rocky clefts is a bird that hides. It lets us understand the bride as a shy creature that a lover must call out, and it shows that the Song's image belongs to Israel's world.

The shepherd 'calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.' The calling voice and the leading out match the beloved's call to 'come away.' Jesus is the voice that people recognize and follow, and the Song's lover is a picture of that pattern.

'I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in.' This is the same picture as the lover at the lattice. The Lord waits, speaks, and promises fellowship to the one who answers, and the promise is of a shared meal.

'The wilderness and the land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose.' The spring of the Song is a small version of the spring the prophet promises for the whole creation. The poem's winter and its end are a sign of God's larger renewal.

'Death has been swallowed up in victory.' The winter that is 'past' in Song 2:11 is a human image of the end of death. Paul's claim is that the seasons of loss are not permanent, and that the last winter has been broken by the resurrection.

God tells Abram to go, using the same form of command as 'come away' in Song 2:10 and 2:13. In both places a love that has chosen someone calls them out of a settled place into a new life, and the response is to go.

A wise teacher looks 'through the lattice' at a young man who is led astray by the wrong woman. A lattice is also where the lover peers in at Song 2:9. The comparison shows that a window can be a place of watching for a snare or for a love, and the difference lies in whom one is drawn to.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is the story of a Creator who keeps seeking those who hide. In the first garden the man and woman hid from the voice of the LORD walking in the breeze of the day, and He called out, 'Where are you?' Genesis 3:8-9. The long history of Israel is a history of a God who goes after His people, and who says through the prophets that He will betroth them to Himself, Hosea 2:19-20. The Song of Songs gives that pursuit a human face: a lover bounding over mountains, standing behind a wall, and asking to hear a voice.

The poem is set in spring, and spring is one of Scripture's pictures of new creation. The Bible begins with a world made in order, and a curse enters it so that thorns and thistles come, Genesis 3:18. The prophets promise that the desert will blossom, Isaiah 35:1, and Paul says that the creation itself 'will be set free from its bondage to decay,' Romans 8:21. The Bible ends in a city and a garden where there is no more death, Revelation 21:4 and 22:2. The winter that is past in the Song is a small sign of that larger turning.

The poem also has a place in the story of redemption. Jesus comes as the bridegroom, Matthew 9:15, and says that He will go and prepare a place and come again, John 14:2-3. The church in this age lives between the call and the arrival. She says, as the bride says in 2:17, 'turn... be like a gazelle,' and the New Testament puts her cry into the final prayer of the Bible, 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The Song's ending note is both belonging, 'my beloved is mine and I am his,' and longing.

The small foxes remind the reader that the story is not finished. Between the invitation and the full day there are things that spoil the vineyard, and the Bible spends many pages on the work of guarding God's people. The prophets, the apostles and the elders in the church are to be watchful, and the Shepherd is the one who keeps.

So the springtime invitation is a signpost in the one story. It tells believers that the God who made the world and was shut out of it has come to the window and called, that the winter of death is ending, and that the answer He is looking for is the one the bride gives: I am yours, and You are mine. The fullness of it waits for the day when the shadows flee and the Bridegroom and the bride are together without a wall.

quiz.q: How is the beloved described as he approaches in 2:8 to 9?

options.text: Coming eagerly, leaping over the mountains like a gazelle or young stag, and standing at the window.
options.note: His approach is swift, glad, and seeking.

options.text: Arriving slowly and reluctantly, unsure whether to come.
options.note: The picture is the opposite: eager, bounding, seeking her out.

options.text: Waiting at a distance for her to come to him first.
options.note: He does pause and stand at the wall, gazing through the windows, yet he is not aloof; he comes bounding to seek her and call her out.

options.text: Hidden and hoping not to be seen.
options.note: He does stand behind the wall and gaze through the lattice, but he is not hiding; he calls to her openly.

quiz.q: What is the heart of the beloved’s invitation in 2:10 to 13?

options.text: The winter is past and spring has come, so arise, my darling, and come away with me.
options.note: It is a summons out of winter into the shared joy of spring.

options.text: A warning that hard times are coming and she should hide.
options.note: The reverse: winter is over and the season of singing has come.

options.text: A request that she stay indoors until he returns.
options.note: He does summon her in view of his coming, but he calls her out into the open to come away, not to stay indoors and wait.

options.text: A list of chores to finish before the harvest.
options.note: The passage does name the blossoming vines and ripening figs, yet it is a lyrical call into springtime love, not a work order.

quiz.q: What do the little foxes of 2:15 picture?

options.text: The small things that quietly spoil love if they are not caught early.
options.note: Foxes gnaw the tender shoots; small compromises ruin a blossoming vineyard.

options.text: Enemies who openly attack the marriage from outside.
options.note: Foxes are indeed a threat to the vineyard of love, but the point is the little foxes, the small and hidden spoilers caught early, not open assault from outside.

options.text: The lovers’ own children.
options.note: The foxes are spoilers of the vineyard, not a picture of children.

options.text: Nothing; it is merely decorative imagery.
options.note: The verse is vivid poetic imagery, yet it carries real wisdom about guarding love from small ruin, so it is not merely decorative.

quiz.q: What does the refrain my beloved is mine and I am his express?

options.text: The glad mutual belonging at the heart of covenant love.
options.note: It is the Song’s heartbeat, echoed again in 6:3.

options.text: That love is a matter of ownership and control.
options.note: The refrain does use the language of belonging, mine and his, but it means glad mutual belonging and delight, not ownership or control.

options.text: A temporary arrangement soon to end.
options.note: It does describe a bond of belonging, but a settled covenant one, not a passing tie soon to end.

options.text: The bride’s wish that she belonged to someone else.
options.note: It is her joyful confession of belonging to this beloved.

quiz.q: How does the seeking, calling beloved point to Christ?

options.text: He pictures Christ who comes seeking His people and calls them out of death’s winter into life.
options.note: The Bridegroom’s voice turns winter to spring, as Christ calls His own by name.

options.text: He teaches that God waits passively for people to find Him.
options.note: The scene does show a God who loves, but a God who comes seeking, as Christ seeks the lost, not one who waits passively.

options.text: He shows that only the strong and swift are loved by God.
options.note: The point is the beloved’s eager seeking, not the merit of the sought.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The scene truly celebrates human love in its own right, yet Scripture reads the Bridegroom’s seeking love as a sign of Christ and His church, so it does point beyond itself.

questions: The beloved comes eagerly, seeking his darling and calling her out. How does it move you to know that God is a seeking God who comes to you rather than waiting at a distance?
Arise and come away, he says, for the winter is past. Where do you need to hear Christ calling you out of a personal winter into new life this season?
The lovers agree to catch the little foxes before they spoil the vineyard. What small compromise or neglect is quietly gnawing at something good in your life or relationships?
My beloved is mine and I am his, she says with settled joy. What would it look like to rest more deeply in belonging to Christ rather than in proving yourself?
The beloved calls the bride his dove hiding in the cliffs, longing to see her face and hear her voice. How might God be inviting you out of hiding and into honest nearness with Him?

translationNotes.note: The season of singing can also be rendered the time of pruning; either way it marks the arrival of spring.
The little foxes that ruin the vineyards is proverbial for the small things that spoil a blossoming love.
The mountains of Bether may name a place or mean the rugged or cleft mountains; the sense is the beloved bounding away over the hills at daybreak.
